paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few types of evidence are as persuasive to a jury as an eyewitness who points to the defendant and says, I will never forget that face. Yet psychological research over four decades has shown that human memory is far more fallible than most people assume. Studies of cases in which DNA evidence later proved convictions wrong found that mistaken eyewitness identification played a part in roughly seventy per cent of them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The central problem is that memory is reconstructive. We do not store events like video recordings; instead, we rebuild them each time we recall them, filling gaps with expectations and information acquired later. In a famous experiment by Elizabeth Loftus, participants watched a film of a car accident and were asked how fast the cars were going when they smashed into each other or, in another group, when they hit each other. Those who heard smashed estimated higher speeds, and a week later, many remembered seeing broken glass although there was none.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Several factors make identifications unreliable. Stress, contrary to popular belief, tends to impair memory for details; the presence of a weapon draws attention away from the perpetrator's face, a phenomenon known as weapon focus. Identifying someone of a different ethnic group is also generally less accurate than identifying someone of one's own. And confidence is a poor guide: witnesses who are certain are only moderately more likely to be correct than those who are hesitant, and their confidence often increases after the police tell them they picked the right person.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Procedures matter too. If police show a witness a single suspect, the witness is more likely to agree than if the suspect appears among several similar people. Suggestive questions can also alter what is remembered. Researchers recommend that identification parades be run by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect, so that he cannot unintentionally signal the answer, and that the witness's initial confidence be recorded before any feedback.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: None of this means that eyewitnesses should be ignored. Accurate memories exist, particularly when conditions are good and procedures careful. The lesson is rather that testimony should be treated as evidence to be assessed, not as proof. Courts in several countries now instruct juries about the limits of memory, and some have reformed identification procedures. For each person wrongly convicted, a guilty person has remained free, and the cost of overconfidence in memory is borne by both.
